title: Sita's prayer to the Ganga
hook: a boat on the Ganga, Sita's prayer in midstream, and a famous boatman who isn't in Valmiki
carry: the Ganga is Ganga Ma, a mother

segments.voice: Yesterday: jata, a vow you can see, twisted into the princes' hair at dawn, after a night when two men shared one grief. Today, across the river.

If you've heard this part of the story at a temple or a family reading, you may remember a boatman who won't let Rama into his boat until he's washed his feet. He's afraid, he says with a grin, that the dust of those feet will turn his wooden boat into a woman, the way it once turned a stone into Ahalya. It's a lovely, funny scene. It comes from a later retelling, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Valmiki's crossing is simpler, with its own quiet center.
screen: `WASH YOUR FEET FIRST.` → `A STORY FROM TULSIDAS.` → `VALMIKI'S CROSSING IS SIMPLER.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, Guha arranges everything. He has a strong boat brought down to the bank, with oarsmen ready. Rama thanks him and says goodbye. Sita steps in first, then Lakshmana, then Rama, and the oarsmen push off into the current. In midstream, Sita folds her hands and speaks to the river itself, to Ganga, as a goddess. She asks Ganga to protect Rama through the fourteen years and bring the three of them back safely, and she vows to worship the river with offerings when they return. The first time the exiles leave dry land, Sita turns the crossing into worship. This is the teaching, and it's still alive. For Hindus, the Ganga is a goddess and a mother as well as a river: Ganga Ma, someone you can speak to. Pilgrims bathe in her and float lamps on her at dusk. Many families keep a small sealed pot of Ganga water at home, to sprinkle at a puja, bless a new house, or give a few drops to someone who is dying. The boat reaches the far bank. Rama sets an order for walking: Lakshmana first, Sita in the middle, Rama last, guarding them both. Guha watches from the shore until they're gone among the trees. So Valmiki's boatman isn't the comic figure of the later story. He's a king and a friend, and the one who stays on the bank, watching.
screen: `GUHA BRINGS A STRONG BOAT.` · `SITA SPEAKS TO THE RIVER.` · `GANGA MA: GODDESS AND MOTHER.` · `LAKSHMANA AHEAD, RAMA BEHIND.` · then, large: `GUHA WATCHES FROM THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: Imagine a small boat in the middle of a wide river, rising a little on each breath in and settling on each breath out. If you pray, do what Sita did: fold your hands, and ask Ganga Ma, or God in your own words, for safe passage for someone you love. If you don't, simply rest between the two shores.
Ganga, the river Hindus honor as Ganga Ma, a goddess and a mother. Sita prays to her in midstream, and Guha watches the exiles disappear into the forest.
Your line: the Ganga is Ganga Ma, a mother. Ahead, a sage where two rivers meet. Until tomorrow.
